pr_comments:
Manage this branch in Squash

Test this branch here: https://mfundulagent-claiming-poc-k69zh.squash.io

There is no discussion of how many connections and how many commands-per-connection in the design that you proposed in #7269 / #7052.

* Why many connections, but only one command per connection? (what is the use-case for this)
* Why is there an exit command if it exits after one command by design?
* Why are you planning to spawn threads for commands? (again, what is the use-case for multiple commands in parallel)

> 
> 
> There is no discussion of how many connections and how many commands-per-connection in the design that you proposed in #7269 / #7052.
> 
>     * Why many connections, but only one command per connection? (what is the use-case for this)
> 

The "connection" is an implementation detail that has to do with the API of libuv (and its implementation underneath, UNIX sockets vs Windows named pipes). Let's just call it many commands.

The use-case is many outstanding commands, as in, many invocations of `netdatacli` so as to facilitate long running commands that are not mutually exclusive. Each invocation of `netdatacli` sends exactly one command. I would reverse the question and ask why do we need a `netdatacli` invocation to issue more than one commands?

>     * Why is there an exit command if it exits after one command by design?
> 

The `exit` command gracefully shuts down the netdata agent. All the commands have to do with `netdata` and not with `netdatacli` itself. Even `help` is not served by `netdatacli` but has to ask `netdata` to fetch a list of commands.

>     * Why are you planning to spawn threads for commands? (again, what is the use-case for multiple commands in parallel)

The idea is that there will be many commands that may run in parallel. One command could take minutes to complete. The event loop of the command server can not block or it will stop serving any other commands that the user may attempt to invoke. Hence, each command is dispatched to the libuv workqueue and the command server event loop remains responsive.

One example let's say is, a cron job issued a database dump and immediately afterwards netdata cloud initiated an agent claiming procedure.

A few suggestions:

1 - After to run the `help` command the agent cannot exit, I think this is the unique command that can never exit when we are inside the terminal.
2 - We need to have an option to specify the destination for `netdatacli`, it will be very interesting from an unique computer to send commands for all netdata inside a network.
3 - This is probably some wrong expectation from my side, but I would like to confirm, when I ran the the command `log rotate`, I was expecting to have more files inside my `/var/log/netdata`, but I continue with exactly the same files, for me this is an error, can you explain us what is expected from this command output?
4 - A suggestion, when we run `python` or `psql` cli commands, when we join the terminal the first thing that we receive is the version of the system that we are connecting, please, add a kind of welcome message that gives information about Netdata.

Finally, you are creating a nice tool, we were needing something like this! :)

> The exit command gracefully shuts down the netdata agent. All the commands have to do with netdata and not with netdatacli itself. Even help is not served by netdatacli but has to ask netdata to fetch a list of commands.

Could we name that command something other than `exit` so that it's less ambiguous what exactly it does?  Usually, when you have a protocol like this, `exit` as a command means you're closing the connection.

Same goes for the 'log rotate' command, the name implies it's rotating the logs itself, but what it's really doing (based on reading the code) is reopening the log files.

Also, I don't know that we really _need_ the `fatal` command unless we want it for debugging.  Most users aren't likely to ever use it (unless there's something I'm missing about `fatal()` being more reliable than a graceful exit, but at that point why not just send SIGABRT (which exists on Windows as well)).

> The "connection" is an implementation detail that has to do with the API of libuv (and its 
> implementation underneath, UNIX sockets vs Windows named pipes). Let's just call it many commands.

It's not really an implementation detail, we can refer to it as "one invocation of the tool" and the question remains the same - why are we doing this way? Is this the best way to supply the functionality - what are the use-cases driving this?

> The use-case is many outstanding commands, as in, many invocations of netdatacli so as to 
> facilitate long running commands that are not mutually exclusive. Each invocation of netdatacli 
> sends exactly one command. I would reverse the question and ask why do we need a 
> netdatacli invocation to issue more than one commands?

Why are we not sending the commands as a sequence from a single invocation of the tool? This is conceptually simpler - there is no spawning of threads to handle things that may be concurrent - and the resulting code is simpler. We've made a decision not to do this way - so what use-case are we supporting by performing concurrent injection of commands rather than sequencing them and waiting for each to terminate?

> The idea is that there will be many commands that may run in parallel. One command could 
> take minutes to complete. The event loop of the command server can not block or it will stop 
> serving any other commands that the user may attempt to invoke. Hence, each command is 
> dispatched to the libuv workqueue and the command server event loop remains responsive.

> One example let's say is, a cron job issued a database dump and immediately afterwards 
> netdata cloud initiated an agent claiming procedure.

So the use-case is that we have multiple CLI-invocations connecting to the agent in parallel for long-running jobs. Yet we have a design where they are all multiplexed onto the same pipe., and we use the EOF on the pipe to trigger the command processing. How are we distinguishing the command/response for each invocation?

> Why are we not sending the commands as a sequence from a single invocation of the tool? This is conceptually simpler - there is no spawning of threads to handle things that may be concurrent - and the resulting code is simpler. We've made a decision not to do this way - so what use-case are we supporting by performing concurrent injection of commands rather than sequencing them and waiting for each to terminate?

Even if we were to allow command sequences like that, we still need to support concurrent execution, because it's well within reason that users might execute more than one command at once (at least, once we have a wider variety of commands).

> Even if we were to allow command sequences like that, we still need to support concurrent 
> execution, because it's well within reason that users might execute more than one command at 
> once (at least, once we have a wider variety of commands).

Yes this is true. I'm exploring whether we are spawning threads at the most appropriate place and whether the design around the use of a pipe is the most appropriate for the target use-cases. The example @mfundul gave above (about the database dump during an agent claiming process) is a very interesting case for considering how we should do this.

About commands such as `log rotate`, this PR just duplicated the existing commands from the agent (as triggered by signals) to the command server. The semantics are identical, If there are complaints about that we have to fix them in the signal handling code as well.

About the interactivity of `netdatacli`, I did not put any effort into that, to be honest. The only reason we have `netdatacli` instead of `nc` or `socat` is because we don't want to create additional dependencies in netdata and for Windows support (`netdatacli` uses libuv which is portable). The idea is that `netdatacli` is mostly going to be used by scripts to perform tasks (e.g. `echo "claim agent token MACHINE_GUID" | netdatacli`). This is going to be too much effort to be like `python`, `psql`, `targetcli` etc. The original intent was to assist with #7086.

We can definitely change some names that are unfortunate. `exit` and `IDEMPOTENT` will have to be something more fitting.

About the server pipe and `EOF`, no message goes over it directly. It works pretty much like a network listener, multiple new client streams are created from that server pipe and this is how we have context per thread and shutting the stream down does not affect the command server.

I understood the goal of the software, when I gave the message suggestion it was because when  we run `netdatacli` we do not have any information on it, let me change the example to clarify my suggestion, we could bring some messages like `/etc/motd` when somebody runs the software, they would know for example that they can call `help` to understand what they have inside the software.

Good work Marko !

The way this works (the client side) is just reading from the pipe and display on screen (just "string" feedback from the server about the command execution) and it works great (does exactly what it needs)

To get extended feedback from the server a quick hack would be to prefix each output from the server with an indicator for example:

- O message
- E message
- P <progress %> 
- X int

So the netdatacli will stdout the "O" prefixed messages, stderr the E ones, and exit with the X code
The P could just make it spin to indicate progress (0 to 100)

issue_context.title: Build cli tool for netdata
issue_context.body:
<!---
When creating a feature request please:
- Verify first that your issue is not already reported on GitHub
- Explain new feature briefly in "Feature idea summary" section
- Provide a clear and concise description of what you expect to happen.
--->

##### Feature idea summary
Build cli tool for netdata. We need a command server in the netdata agent and a cli utility so that we can communicate with the agent from the command line. Signals are insufficient to do that because they are limited in number, they do not carry any information and they are not cross-platform. This is described in #7052 and will help implement #7086.
comments:
> network sockets: there is no easy and obvious security model with networking even though its low performance is not likely to be an issue since we don't intend to use commands in rapid succession.

We have ACLs on the incoming web sockets. Adding a capability for "cli" would allow it to be bound to `localhost`, and the commands could then go through the existing v1/api despatch. What were the security problems with this approach? - I did not understand why you ruled it out.

It would allow us to use `curl` as the local CLI instead of writing a new tool.
You may choose to disable the web part so I think cli needs another way to issue commands.
Do you mean disabling the dashboard or disabling the internal server completely?

> 
> 
> > network sockets: there is no easy and obvious security model with networking even though its low performance is not likely to be an issue since we don't intend to use commands in rapid succession.
> 
> We have ACLs on the incoming web sockets. Adding a capability for "cli" would allow it to be bound to `localhost`, and the commands could then go through the existing v1/api despatch. What were the security problems with this approach? - I did not understand why you ruled it out.
> 
> It would allow us to use `curl` as the local CLI instead of writing a new tool.

"cli" is a completely new path that:
- talks directly to the daemon and does not have to go through the web API
- is capable of doing low level operations such as stopping the daemon or the web server etc.
- is using dead simple rock solid file based permissions, zero configuration needed
- you don't really have to write a new tool, `nc` and `socat` already do all the work

Two quick thoughts on this:

* Signals that currently work should continue to work on platforms they can be supported on, and the CLI tool should probably fall back to signals for things it can if it fails to contact Netdata through whatever other means it's using.
* It sounds like you're thinking of using UNIX sockets. Keep in mind that that essentially won't work on many Windows systems.  `AF_UNIX` is only supported on new enough Windows 10 systems (April 2018 update or newer), and lacks some features (only supports `SOCK_STREAM`, not `SOCK_DGRAM` or `SOCK_SEQPACKET`, no ancillary data (so no `SCM_CREDENTIALS` or similar), no autobind, and no `socketpair` API). So this needs to be thought through properly to make sure it won't make it harder to support Windows in the future.

> 
> 
> Two quick thoughts on this:
> 
>     * Signals that currently work should continue to work on platforms they can be supported on, and the CLI tool should probably fall back to signals for things it can if it fails to contact Netdata through whatever other means it's using.
> 

For sure, this is already the case in the proof of concept in PR #7255

>     * It sounds like you're thinking of using UNIX sockets. Keep in mind that that essentially won't work on many Windows systems.  `AF_UNIX` is only supported on new enough Windows 10 systems (April 2018 update or newer), and lacks some features (only supports `SOCK_STREAM`, not `SOCK_DGRAM` or `SOCK_SEQPACKET`, no ancillary data (so no `SCM_CREDENTIALS` or similar), no autobind, and no `socketpair` API). So this needs to be thought through properly to make sure it won't make it harder to support Windows in the future.

It's libuv named pipes. More details here: https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/7052#issuecomment-549891013
@mfundul and I had a very in-depth technical analysis and discussion of the issues in implementing and testing. We have arrived at the stimate of 5.1 so we will call it a five.

review_comments: Has this been tested on windows?
No.
To clarify, netdata does not work with Windows, the porting will take many months, I am just trying to be proactive here to minimize the porting effort.
Then this line should be commented out and a #error should indicate that whoever is porting to windows needs to check this.

This seems quite dangerous - it puts a lot of assumptions on the behaviour of high-priority commands so that they cannot trip over anything else that is running (including exclusive commands).

If this is only designed to let the help command execute quickly then can we do it a different way - a status message that the agent is currently busy and the command will execute when possible would be safer.
Are you assuming that the pipe writes faster than stdin receives lines of text? This might not be true in a script and there is no feedback from `pipe_write_cb()` to control the speed of this loop.
The `cli` will only handle one line of text. You call it again to run a different command.
I'll resolve this here as otherwise the interface is messy, but I've picked this up in the main discussion thread further down.
Missing new line here.
This is not good tonight - please no syntax. This must be closed.
Is this where we would lock mutexes for the actual command and despatch into the daemon?
Any mutexes will be called after thread spawning so as to not block the event loop.
If we only handle commands when the pipe closes then this will work like a batch interface instead of a CLI. Is this the intention?
Each invocation of `cli` issues exactly one command.
This is only called during shutdown. How do we handle status results coming back from commands - i.e.claiming succeeded or failed?
They are handled fine. The shutdown will only affect the send side.
I didn't think that we supported multiple client connections - either this should trigger an error or we should separate state for multiple connections.
We have separate state indeed.

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3385515/static-assert-in-c

We don't need a dummy function to do our own version of assert. There is a standard way to do it in C11.

This implies that the command server allows exactly one command per connection - but the positioning of the call-backs in the sequence, the mutexes and the dynamic allocation of memory inside `parse_commands` suggest otherwise.
Basic design questions:
* How many active connections are allowed?
* How many commands are allowed over each connection?

If the answers are "one" and "one" then the code is too complex and needs to be simplified. If the answers are different then it's unclear why the parsing is being triggered at the end of the pipe read and the connection closed after execution of a command.

Active connections can be many.

The parsing is triggered at the end because each command sends an EOF. The connection is closed only after the status is sent back to `cli`, which will be after the command execution.
This doesn't check the result of the call - why is there a result?
I will have to add error messages depending on the return value.
Made it void.

Why are you putting this inside the enum and then adding BUGON later with a compile-time expression? It looks like it would be easier to just` #define (sizeof(command_info_array) / sizeof(command_info_t))`. Adding something that can go wrong, and then a `sanity_check` to stop it is not as simple as just not letting it go wrong.

This enum indexes various data structures, it's not just a part of `command_info_array[]` (e.g. `execute_command(CMD_SAVE_DATABASE, NULL, NULL);` in `signals.c`). Hence it exists.

As a result, there is nothing stopping a developer from modifying the definition of `command_info_array[]` (e.g. add a line). The `sanity_check()` is the only way to catch the bug at compile time and preserve consistency.
If you `#define CMD_TOTAL_COMMANDS (sizeof(command_info_array) / sizeof(command_info_t))` then a dev can no longer break it in that way.

Having mutexes on each command makes sense, as it stops a collision with the signal handling code in the daemon. This doesn't make any sense to me. Why do we want to stop two idempotent commands from running at the same time, or two high-priority commands.. ?
The one case it would make sense for if the command type is exclusive, it does not make sense for the the types.

It's a reader-writer lock. The commands are not stopped because they are readers. The only writer is a command of exclusive type . The mutexes exist only for orthogonal commands and they are command specific.
